Polynomials Counting Group Colorings in Graphs

Houshan Fu

School of Mathematics and Information Science

Guangzhou University

Guangzhou 510006, Guangdong, P. R. China

Email: fuhoushan@gzhu.edu.cn

Abstract

Jaeger et al. in 1992 introduced group coloring as the dual concept to group connectivity in graphs. Let Γ\Gamma be an Abelian group, f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma and DD an orientation of a graph GG. A vertex coloring c:V⁡(G)→Γc:V(G)\to\Gamma is a (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-coloring if c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)≠f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)\neq f(e) for each edge e=u​ve=uv and the corresponding arc D⁡(e)=(u,v)D(e)=(u,v) directed from uu to vv. We introduce the concept of α\alpha-compatible graphs and define the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) at kk in terms of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs, where α\alpha is an assigning of GG from its cycles to {0,1}\{0,1\}. We prove that the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) equals the number of (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings for any Abelian group Γ\Gamma of order kk and f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma such that the assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} induced by ff equals α\alpha. In particular, P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) is the classical chromatic polynomial if α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for any cycle CC of GG. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of α\alpha-compatible broken cycles and interpret P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) in terms of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs that do not contain α\alpha-compatible broken cycles. This implies that the absolute value of the coefficient of kr⁡(G)−ik^{r(G)-i} in P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) equals the number of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs that have ii edges and contain no α\alpha-compatible broken cycles, which generalizes the Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem. Based on the combinatorial explanation, we establish a unified order-preserving relation from assignings to cycle-assigning polynomials. Finally, we show that for any loopless graphs GG, the coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) are nonzero and alternate in sign, and further conjecture that the sequence of absolute values of its coefficients is unimodal and log-concave.

Keywords: Graph coloring, chromatic polynomial, α\alpha-compatible graph, broken cycle


Mathematics Subject Classifications: 05C31, 05C15

1 Introduction

The graphs G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=\big(V(G),E(G)\big) with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) and edge set E⁡(G)E(G) considered in this paper are finite, allowing multiple edges and loops. A more general setting and background on graphs can be found in the books [4]. An orientation of a graph is an assignment of direction to each edge. In this context, each oriented edge is referred to as an arc. An oriented graph arises from a graph GG together with a particular orientation DD, denoted by D⁡(G):=(V⁡(D),A⁡(D))D(G):=\big(V(D),A(D)\big), where A⁡(D)A(D) is the collection of arcs with respect to the orientation DD and V⁡(D)=V⁡(G)V(D)=V(G).

Graph coloring is a significant subfield in graph theory that originated in the middle of the 19th century with the famous Four Color Problem. A kk-vertex coloring, or simply a kk-coloring, of GG is a mapping c:V⁡(G)→Sc:V(G)\to S, where SS is a set of distinct kk colors, typically S={1,2,…,k}S=\{1,2,...,k\}. A vertex coloring is said to be proper if no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

We consider finite additive Abelian groups Γ\Gamma with the identity 00 as coloring sets in this paper. Jaeger, Linial, Payan and Tarsi [12] introduced the concept of group coloring as the dual concept of group connectivity of graphs in 1992. Group connectivity and group colorings of graphs are nicely surveyed in [16]. Let f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma be a function. With an orientation DD of GG, a vertex coloring c:V⁡(G)→Γc:V(G)\to\Gamma is called a (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-coloring if c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)≠f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)\neq f(e) for each arc D⁡(e)=(u,v)∈A⁡(D)D(e)=(u,v)\in A(D), where the edge e=u​ve=uv and (u,v)(u,v) denotes the arc D⁡(e)D(e) directed from uu to vv. In particular, when f=0f=0, (Γ,0)(\Gamma,0)-coloring is exactly the ordinary proper coloring. Furthermore, GG is said to be Γ\Gamma-colorable under the orientation DD if for any function f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma, GG always admits a (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-coloring. Since then, topics related to group coloring problems have attracted a lot of research attentions, such as [14, 19, 20, 21, 15, 17, 18]. Their primary focus is on the (weak) group chromatic number and related group coloring problems, such as whether a graph that is Γ1\Gamma_{1}-colorable for some Abelian group Γ1\Gamma_{1} is also Γ2\Gamma_{2}-colorable for any Abelian group Γ2\Gamma_{2} of the same order. However, another fundamental problem of counting (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings has been overlooked. In this paper, we introduce the cycle-assigning polynomial that counts the number of (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings of graphs, and investigate its fundamental properties, particularly focusing on its coefficients.

A fundamental problem in graph theory is determining the chromatic number of a graph, which refers to the smallest integer kk such that the graph admits a proper coloring with kk colors. Counting proper colorings can be seen as another facet of this problem. In an attempt to address the long-standing Four Color Problem, Birkhoff [2] discovered that the number of proper colorings of a planar GG with kk colors is a polynomial in kk, called the chromatic polynomial. Twenty years later, Whitney [26, 27] extended the concept of the chromatic polynomial to general graphs and gave a combinatorial description of its coefficients by introducing the broken cycle, now famously known as the Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem. Since then, various generalizations of this theorem have been developed across different mathematical structures, such as matroids [5, 8], lattices [3, 24], hyperplane arrangements [22], hypergraphs [6]. See [7] for more related work. Motivated by their work, it is natural to ask the two questions:

  • •

    Is there a polynomial function of |Γ||\Gamma| that generalize the chromatic polynomial and counts (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings in graphs?

  • •

    Can we provide a combinatorial interpretation for the coefficients of the polynomial function?

To answer the first question, we propose the concept of an α\alpha-compatible graph. A cycle CC of GG is a connected 2-regular subgraph of GG. The corresponding edge set E⁡(C)E(C) is referred to as a circuit of GG. Let 𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G) be the family of cycles of GG. An assigning α\alpha of GG is a mapping from 𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G) to the set {0,1}\{0,1\}. In particular, we define α=0\alpha=0 when GG does not contain cycles, i.e., 𝒞⁡(G)=∅\mathcal{C}(G)=\emptyset.

Definition 1.1.

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG. A graph GG is said to be α\alpha-compatible if α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for every cycle CC in GG. Furthermore, a subgraph HH of GG is called an α\alpha-compatible subgraph if the restriction of α\alpha to HH satisfies α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for all cycles CC in HH. In this sense, HH is αH\alpha_{H}-compatible, where αH\alpha_{H} is the restriction of α\alpha to HH defined by αH​(C):=α​(C)\alpha_{H}(C):=\alpha(C) for all C∈𝒞⁡(H)C\in\mathcal{C}(H).

Let f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma, and P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big) be the number of (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings of GG with an orientation DD. We first provide an explicit formula for the counting function P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big) in terms of the α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph expansion in Theorem 2.1, where α\alpha equals the admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} induced by ff. For a detailed definition of an admissible assigning, see Section 2. Inspired by this expression, we define a cycle-assigning polynomial in terms of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs. It turns out that cycle-assigning polynomials precisely count (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings of graphs, as shown in Theorem 2.2.

Definition 1.2.

For any assigning α\alpha of GG, the cycle-assigning polynomial of GG in kk is defined as

P⁡(G,α,k):=∑H is an α-compatiblespanning subgraph of G(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H),P(G,\alpha;k):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mbox{$H$ is an $\alpha$-compatible}\\ \mbox{spanning subgraph of $G$}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)},

where c⁡(H)c(H) is the number of components of HH.

To address the second question, we introduce the concept of an α\alpha-compatible broken cycle as an extension of the usual broken cycle. In Theorem 3.2, we demonstrate that the unsigned coefficients of cycle-assigning polynomials can be expressed in terms of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs that do not contain α\alpha-compatible broken cycles. This extends the Whitney’s classical Broken Cycle Theorem [26]. Based on the counting interpretation, we further establish a unified order-preserving relation from assignings to cycle-assigning polynomials when both are naturally ordered in Theorem 4.1. In addition, we also provides a new perspective on addressing certain group coloring problems in graphs. A detailed discussion will appear at the end of Section 4.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents an explicit formula for calculating (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings (see Theorem 2.1), and further shows that the number of (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings with the function ff corresponding to an assigning is evaluated by the cycle-assigning polynomial of |Γ||\Gamma| in Theorem 3.2. In Section 3, we show that the cycle-assigning polynomial can be interpreted in terms of the α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs that do not contain α\alpha-compatible broken cycles in Theorem 3.2, which generalizes the Whitney’s classical Broken Cycle Theorem and is called the Generalized Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem. Section 4 utilizes the Generalized Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem to establish a unified order-preserving relation from assignings to cycle-assigning polynomials in Theorem 4.1, demonstrates that for any loopless graphs, the coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) are nonzero and alternate in sign Corollary 4.2, and conjecture that the absolute values of its coefficients form a unimodal and log-concave sequence in Conjecture 4.3.

2 Cycle-assigning polynomials

In this section, we focus on the study of cycle-assigning polynomials, exploring their structural properties and their role in counting (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings. Let us review some necessary notations and definitions on graphs. A graph HH is a subgraph of GG if V⁡(H)⊆V⁡(G)V(H)\subseteq V(G) and E⁡(H)⊆E⁡(G)E(H)\subseteq E(G). When E⁡(H)=E⁡(G)E(H)=E(G), the subgraph HH of GG is referred to as a spanning subgraph. For an edge subset S⊆E⁡(G)S\subseteq E(G), G−SG-S is the subgraph obtained by removing the edges in SS. Denote by G​⟨S⟩G\langle S\rangle the spanning subgraph with edges SS, that is, G⁡⟨S⟩=G−(E⁡(G)∖S)G\langle S\rangle=G-(E(G)\smallsetminus S). Conversely, suppose HH is a proper subgraph containing no edge e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), we denote by H+eH+e the subgraph of GG by adding the edge ee. In addition, if ee is not a loop of GG, the graph G/eG/e is obtained by contracting ee, that is, identifying the ends of ee to create a single new vertex and then removing ee.

Let 𝒪⁡(G)\mathcal{O}(G) be the set of all orientations of GG. Unless otherwise stated, we always choose an arbitrary but fixed reference orientation DD for GG. For each cycle CC of GG, define a map σD⁡(C)\sigma_{D(C)} from the circuit E⁡(C)E(C) to the set {1,−1}\{1,-1\} as

σD⁡(C)​(e):={1,if the direction of the arc D⁡(e) is clockwise with respect to C;−1,if the direction of the arc D⁡(e) is counter-clockwise with respect to C.\sigma_{D(C)}(e):=\begin{cases}1,&\mbox{if the direction of the arc $D(e)$ is clockwise with respect to $C$};\\ -1,&\mbox{if the direction of the arc $D(e)$ is counter-clockwise with respect to $C$}.\end{cases}

Notably, each function f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma automatically induces an assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} on 𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G) such that for each cycle CC of GG,

αD,f​(C)={0, if ​∑e∈E⁡(C)σD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=0;1, otherwise .\alpha_{D,f}(C)=\begin{cases}0,&\mbox{ if }\sum_{e\in E(C)}\sigma_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=0;\\ 1,&\mbox{ otherwise }.\end{cases}

We say that α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f} is DD-admissible, or simply admissible.

Recall from Section 1 that the counting function P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big) is the number of (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings of GG associated with the orientation DD and a function f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma. To derive an explicit formula for the counting function P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big), we need to introduce the Möbius Inversion Formula in [4, Theorem 2.25]. The Möbius Inversion Formula states that if the function g:2E⁡(G)→Γg:2^{E(G)}\to\Gamma is defined as

g⁡(S):=∑S⊆X⊆E⁡(G)h⁡(X) for ∀S⊆E⁡(G),g(S):=\sum_{S\subseteq X\subseteq E(G)}h(X)\quad\mbox{ for }\quad\forall\,S\subseteq E(G),

then, for all S⊆E⁡(G)S\subseteq E(G),

h⁡(S)=∑S⊆X⊆E⁡(G)(−1)|X|−|S|​g​(X),h(S)=\sum_{S\subseteq X\subseteq E(G)}(-1)^{|X|-|S|}g(X), (2.1)

where hh is a function from the family 2E⁡(G)2^{E(G)} of all edge subsets of GG to Γ\Gamma.

The following result shows that the counting function P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big) can be expressed in terms of the αD,f\alpha_{D,f}-compatible spanning subgraph expansion.

Theorem 2.1 (Counting Formula).

Let f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma and α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f}. Then

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=∑H is an α-compatiblespanning subgraph of G(−1)|E⁡(H)|​|Γ|c⁡(H),P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mbox{$H$ is an $\alpha$-compatible}\\ \mbox{spanning subgraph of $G$}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}|\Gamma|^{c(H)},

where c⁡(H)c(H) is the number of components of the spanning subgraph HH of GG.

Proof.

For any S⊆E⁡(G)S\subseteq E(G), let CS​(D​(G),f,Γ)C_{S}\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big) be the number of vertex colorings c:V⁡(G)→Γc:V(G)\to\Gamma such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for each edge e=u​v∈Se=uv\in S with D⁡(e)=(u,v)D(e)=(u,v), and PS​(D​(G),f,Γ)P_{S}(D(G),f;\Gamma) be the number of vertex colorings c:V⁡(G)→Γc:V(G)\to\Gamma such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for each edge e=u​v∈Se=uv\in S with D⁡(e)=(u,v)D(e)=(u,v) and c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)≠f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)\neq f(e) for each edge e=u​v∈E⁡(G)∖Se=uv\in E(G)\smallsetminus S with D⁡(e)=(u,v)D(e)=(u,v). Then we have

CS​(D⁡⟨S⟩,f,Γ)=CS​(D⁡(G),f,Γ),P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=P∅​(D⁡(G),f,Γ)C_{S}\big(D\langle S\rangle,f;\Gamma\big)=C_{S}\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big),\quad\quad P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=P_{\emptyset}\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)

and

C∅​(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=∑S⊆E⁡(G)PS​(D⁡(G),f,Γ).C_{\emptyset}\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq E(G)}P_{S}\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big).

It follows from (2.1) that

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=∑S⊆E⁡(G)(−1)|S|​CS​(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=∑S⊆E⁡(G)(−1)|S|​CS​(D⁡⟨S⟩,f,Γ).P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq E(G)}(-1)^{|S|}C_{S}\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq E(G)}(-1)^{|S|}C_{S}\big(D\langle S\rangle,f;\Gamma\big). (2.2)

In addition, [13, Proposition 2.2] demonstrates that GG admits a vertex coloring cc such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for any e=u​v∈E⁡(G)e=uv\in E(G) with D⁡(e)=(u,v)D(e)=(u,v) if and only if the function ff satisfies the condition ∑e∈E⁡(C)σD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=0\sum_{e\in E(C)}\sigma_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=0 for every cycle CC of GG. This condition is equivalent to α⁡(C)=0\alpha(C)=0 for all cycles CC of GG since α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f}. Therefore, CS​(D⁡⟨S⟩,f,Γ)=0C_{S}\big(D\langle S\rangle,f;\Gamma\big)=0 whenever G​⟨S⟩G\langle S\rangle is an α\alpha-incompatible subgraph of GG. Then, P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big) in (2.2) can be simplified to the following form

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=∑S⊆E⁡(G),G​⟨S⟩​ is αG​⟨S⟩-compatible(−1)|S|​CS​(D⁡⟨S⟩,f,Γ).P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq E(G),\\ G\langle S\rangle\mbox{ is $\alpha_{G\langle S\rangle}$-compatible}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S|}C_{S}\big(D\langle S\rangle,f;\Gamma\big). (2.3)

Denote by CS​(D⁡⟨S⟩,fS,Γ)C_{S}\big(D\langle S\rangle,f_{S};\Gamma\big) the collection of vertex colorings c:V⁡(G)→Γc:V(G)\to\Gamma of G​⟨S⟩G\langle S\rangle such that c⁡(v)−c⁡(u)=f⁡(e)c(v)-c(u)=f(e) for each edge e=u​v∈Se=uv\in S with D⁡(e)=(u,v)D(e)=(u,v). P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=∑S⊆E⁡(G),G​⟨S⟩​ is αG​⟨S⟩-compatible(−1)|S|​|Γ|c⁡(G​⟨S⟩),P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq E(G),\\ G\langle S\rangle\mbox{ is $\alpha_{G\langle S\rangle}$-compatible}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S|}|\Gamma|^{c(G\langle S\rangle)},

which completes the proof. ∎

As a direct consequence of Theorem 2.1, the cycle-assigning polynomials corresponding to admissible assignings precisely count the number of (Γ,f)(\Gamma,f)-colorings of GG for any Abelian group Γ\Gamma and function f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma.

Theorem 2.2.

Let α\alpha be an admissible assigning of GG. Then P⁡(G,α,k)=P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)P(G,\alpha;k)=P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big) for every orientation D∈𝒪⁡(G)D\in\mathcal{O}(G), every Abelian group Γ\Gamma of order kk and every function f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma satisfying αD,f=α\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha.

By applying Theorem 2.2, we obtain the next corollary, which states that the number of (G,f)(G,f)-colorings depends only on αD,f\alpha_{D,f}, and not on the structure of Γ\Gamma and the choice of the orientation DD.

Corollary 2.3.

Let D,D′∈𝒪⁡(G)D,D^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}(G), Γ,Γ′\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime} be two Abelian groups of the same order and functions f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma, f′:E⁡(G)→Γ′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to\Gamma^{\prime}. If αD,f=αD′,f′\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}}, then P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=P⁡(D′​(G),f′,Γ′)P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=P\big(D^{\prime}(G),f^{\prime};\Gamma^{\prime}\big).

Proof.

By Theorem 2.2, we have

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=P⁡(G,α,k)=P⁡(D′​(G),f′,Γ′),P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=P(G,\alpha;k)=P\big(D^{\prime}(G),f^{\prime};\Gamma^{\prime}\big),

where α=αD,f=αD′,f′\alpha=\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}}. ∎

We further explore the fundamental properties of cycle-assigning polynomials. Suppose e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G) is not a loop of GG. Then the set 𝒞⁡(G/e)\mathcal{C}(G/e) of cycles of G/eG/e consists of the following two parts:

𝒞−e(G):={C∈𝒞(G/e):C∈𝒞(G),e∉E(C)},𝒞/e(G/e):={C/e:C∈𝒞(G),e∈E(C)}.\mathcal{C}_{-e}(G):=\big\{C\in\mathcal{C}(G/e):C\in\mathcal{C}(G),e\notin E(C)\big\},\;\mathcal{C}_{/e}(G/e):=\big\{C/e:C\in\mathcal{C}(G),e\in E(C)\big\}.

In this sense, each assigning α\alpha of GG induces an assigning αG/e\alpha_{G/e} of G/eG/e, where αG/e​(C):=α​(C)\alpha_{G/e}(C):=\alpha(C) for C∈𝒞−e​(G)C\in\mathcal{C}_{-e}(G) and αG/e​(C/e):=α⁡(C)\alpha_{G/e}(C/e):=\alpha(C) for C∈𝒞⁡(G)C\in\mathcal{C}(G) containing ee. We first obtain a deletion-contraction formula for general cycle-assigning polynomials, which provides an inductive approach to proving the Generalized Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem (see Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 2.4 (Deletion-contraction Formula).

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG. Then

P⁡(G,α,k)={k−1k​P​(G−e,αG−e,k), if ​e​ is a bridge;0, if ​e​ is a loop and ​α​(e)=0;P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k), if ​e​ is a loop and ​α​(e)=1;P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)−P⁡(G/e,αG/e,k), otherwise.P(G,\alpha;k)=\begin{cases}\frac{k-1}{k}P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k),&\mbox{ if }e\mbox{ is a bridge};\\ 0,&\mbox{ if }e\mbox{ is a loop and }\alpha(e)=0;\\ P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k),&\mbox{ if }e\mbox{ is a loop and }\alpha(e)=1;\\ P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)-P(G/e,\alpha_{G/e};k),&\mbox{ otherwise}.\end{cases}
Proof.

Let 𝒮e\mathcal{S}_{e} be the family of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing ee and 𝒮−e\mathcal{S}_{-e} be the family of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that do not contain ee. If ee is a bridge, then a subgraph HH containing ee is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG if and only if H−eH-e is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG. Therefore, we conclude that every α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph HH of GG containing ee gives rise to a unique α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph H−eH-e of GG that does not contain ee, and vice versa. Then we have

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑H∈𝒮−e(−1)|E⁡(H+e)|​kc⁡(H+e)+∑H∈𝒮−e(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H).P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}}(-1)^{|E(H+e)|}k^{c(H+e)}+\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}.

Since ee is a bridge, c⁡(H+e)=c⁡(H)−1c(H+e)=c(H)-1 for any H∈𝒮−eH\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}. Hence, we deduce

P⁡(G,α,k)=k−1k​P​(G−e,αG−e,k).P(G,\alpha;k)=\frac{k-1}{k}P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k).

If ee is a loop, we need to consider both cases: α⁡(e)=0\alpha(e)=0 and α⁡(e)=1\alpha(e)=1. For the former case, similarly to the case where ee is a bridge, we can easily derive P⁡(G,α,k)=0P(G,\alpha;k)=0. For the latter case, it is clear that HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG if and only if HH is an αG−e\alpha_{G-e}-compatible spanning subgraph of G−eG-e. So, we arrive at P⁡(G,α,k)=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k).

If ee is neither a bridge nor a loop, then HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing no ee if and only if HH is an αG−e\alpha_{G-e}-compatible spanning subgraph of G−eG-e, and HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing ee if and only if H/eH/e is an αG/e\alpha_{G/e}-compatible spanning subgraph of G/eG/e. Therefore, we have

P⁡(G,α,k)\displaystyle P(G,\alpha;k) =∑H∈𝒮−e(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)+∑H∈𝒮e(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)\displaystyle=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{-e}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}+\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}
=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)+∑H∈𝒮e(−1)|E⁡(H/e)|+1​kc⁡(H/e)\displaystyle=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)+\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}(-1)^{|E(H/e)|+1}k^{c(H/e)}
=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)−P⁡(G/e,αG/e,k),\displaystyle=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)-P(G/e,\alpha_{G/e};k),

which finishes the proof. ∎

In addition, the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) has the following simple decomposition formula.

Theorem 2.5.

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG and G=G1⊔G2⊔⋯⊔GiG=G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup G_{i}, where GjG_{j} is the component of GG for j=1,2,…,ij=1,2,\ldots,i. Then

P⁡(G,α,k)=∏j=1iP⁡(Gj,αGj,k).P(G,\alpha;k)=\prod_{j=1}^{i}P(G_{j},\alpha_{G_{j}};k).
Proof.

Since GG decomposes into the union of the components GjG_{j} of GG, each α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG is partitioned into the disjoint union of the αGj\alpha_{G_{j}}-compatible spanning subgraph of GjG_{j}, and vice versa. Therefore, we can deduce P⁡(G,α,k)=∏j=1iP⁡(Gj,αGj,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=\prod_{j=1}^{i}P(G_{j},\alpha_{G_{j}};k), which finishes the proof. ∎

At the end of the section, we list the cycle-assigning polynomials for the empty graph, a tree and the cycle on nn vertices.

Example 2.6.
  • (1)

    Let OnO_{n} be the empty graph on nn vertices. Then α=0\alpha=0 and

    P⁡(On,0,k)=P⁡(On,k)=kn.P(O_{n},0;k)=P(O_{n};k)=k^{n}.
  • (2)

    Let TnT_{n} be a tree on nn vertices. Then α=0\alpha=0 and

    P⁡(Tn,0,k)=P⁡(Tn,k)=k​(k−1)n−1=∑i=1n(−1)n−i​(n−1i−1)​ki.P(T_{n},0;k)=P(T_{n};k)=k(k-1)^{n-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{n-i}\binom{n-1}{i-1}k^{i}.
  • (3)

    Let CnC_{n} be a cycle on nn vertices. Combining part (2) and Theorem 2.4, we have

    P⁡(Cn,α,k)​{(k−1)n+(−1)n​(k−1), if ​α​(Cn)=0;(k−1)n+(−1)n+1, if ​α​(Cn)=1.P(C_{n},\alpha;k)\begin{cases}(k-1)^{n}+(-1)^{n}(k-1),&\mbox{ if }\alpha(C_{n})=0;\\ (k-1)^{n}+(-1)^{n+1},&\mbox{ if }\alpha(C_{n})=1.\end{cases}

3 Generalization of Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem

A natural question is whether there is a combinatorial interpretation for the coefficients of cycle-assigning polynomials. To address this, we introduce the concept of an α\alpha-compatible broken cycle as an extension of the usual broken cycle.

Definition 3.1.

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG and ≺\prec be a total order on E⁡(G)E(G). We say that a subgraph HH of GG is said to be:

  • •

    an α\alpha-compatible cycle of GG if HH is a cycle and α⁡(H)=0\alpha(H)=0;

  • •

    an α\alpha-compatible broken cycle of GG if HH is obtained from an α\alpha-compatible cycle by removing the maximal element with respect to the total order ≺\prec.

The following result expresses the coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) in terms of the α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs that do not contain α\alpha-compatible broken cycles, which is an extended version of the Whitney’s celebrated Broken Cycle Theorem given by Whitney [26]. It is worth noting that the coefficients wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) in Theorem 3.2 are independent of the choice of edge order.

Theorem 3.2 (Generalized Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem).

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG and ≺\prec a total order on E⁡(G)E(G). Write P⁡(G,α,k)=∑i=0r⁡(G)(−1)i​wi​(G,α)​k|V⁡(G)|−iP(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{i=0}^{r(G)}(-1)^{i}w_{i}(G,\alpha)k^{|V(G)|-i}, where r⁡(G)=|V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G)r(G)=|V(G)|-c(G). Then each unsigned coefficient wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) is the number of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that have exactly ii edges and do not contain α\alpha-compatible broken cycles with respect to ≺\prec.

Proof.

Let E(G)={e1≺e2≺⋯≺em}E(G)=\{e_{1}\prec e_{2}\prec\cdots\prec e_{m}\}. We prove the result by induction on mm. If m=0m=0, there is nothing to prove. Suppose m≥1m\geq 1 and the result holds for smaller values of mm. Let em=u​ve_{m}=uv. If eme_{m} is a loop and α⁡(em)=0\alpha(e_{m})=0, it is trivial via Theorem 2.4. If eme_{m} is a loop and α⁡(em)=1\alpha(e_{m})=1, from

P⁡(G,α,k)=P⁡(G−e,αG−e,k)P(G,\alpha;k)=P(G-e,\alpha_{G-e};k)

in Theorem 2.4, the result holds in this case by the inductive hypothesis.

Finally, if eme_{m} is neither a bridge nor a loop, by the inductive hypothesis, the result holds for both graphs G−emG-e_{m} and G/emG/e_{m}. With a slight abuse of notation, we identify E(G/em)={e1≺e2≺⋯≺em−1}E(G/e_{m})=\{e_{1}\prec e_{2}\prec\cdots\prec e_{m-1}\}. More specifically, by identifying the ends of eme_{m}, this create a single new vertex of G/emG/e_{m}, denoted by vemv_{e_{m}}. Suppose the edge ei=x​ye_{i}=xy in GG for some i<mi<m. If neither xx nor yy is one of the vertices uu or vv, then eie_{i} automatically remains an edge in G/emG/e_{m}. If either xx or yy is one of the vertices uu or vv, we identity eie_{i} as u​vemuv_{e_{m}}, vem​vv_{e_{m}}v or vem​vemv_{e_{m}}v_{e_{m}} depending on the incidence of eie_{i} in GG.

By the Deletion-contraction Formula in Theorem 2.4, we have w0​(G,α)=w0​(G−em,αG−em)w_{0}(G,\alpha)=w_{0}(G-e_{m},\alpha_{G-e_{m}}) and

wi(G,α)=wi(G−em,αG−em)+wi−1(G/em,αG/em),i=1,2,…,r(G).w_{i}(G,\alpha)=w_{i}(G-e_{m},\alpha_{G-e_{m}})+w_{i-1}(G/e_{m},\alpha_{G/e_{m}}),\;i=1,2,\ldots,r(G). (3.1)

Therefore, to complete the induction step, it is sufficient to check that the relation in (3.1) is true. But this is a consequence of the following two simple facts: (a) HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph HH of GG that does not contain ee and α\alpha-compatible broken cycles if and only if HH is an αG−em\alpha_{G-e_{m}}-compatible spanning subgraph of G−emG-e_{m} that does not contain αG−em\alpha_{G-e_{m}}-compatible broken cycles; (b) HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph HH of GG that contains ee and no α\alpha-compatible broken cycles if and only if H/emH/e_{m} is an αG/em\alpha_{G/e_{m}}-compatible spanning subgraph of G/emG/e_{m} that does not contain αG/em\alpha_{G/e_{m}}-compatible broken cycles. So, we complete the proof. ∎

Furthermore, when α\alpha is an admissible assigning of GG, we will provide another direct proof of Theorem 3.2. For this purpose, the next lemma is required.

Lemma 3.3.

Let α\alpha be a DD-admissible assigning of GG and ≺\prec a total order on E⁡(G)E(G). Suppose HH is a subgraph of GG containing an α\alpha-compatible broken cycle BB and B=C−eCB=C-e_{C} for some α\alpha-compatible cycle CC of GG, where eCe_{C} is the maximal member in E⁡(C)E(C) with respect to ≺\prec. If HH is an α\alpha-compatible subgraph of GG and eC∉E⁡(H)e_{C}\notin E(H), then H+eCH+e_{C} is also an α\alpha-compatible subgraph of GG.

Proof.

Note that CC is a cycle in H+eCH+e_{C}, but not in HH. If H+eCH+e_{C} contains exactly one more cycle CC than HH, there is nothing left to prove. Otherwise, H+eCH+e_{C} contains at least one additional cycle compared to HH, excluding the cycle CC. Notably, every such additional cycle, together with the cycle CC, forms a θ\theta-subgraph in H+eCH+e_{C}. Therefore, this case reduces to verifying that each such θ\theta-subgraph in H+eCH+e_{C} is an α\alpha-compatible subgraph of GG. Notice that α\alpha is a DD-admissible assigning of GG. Without loss of generality, we only need to examine the following oriented θ\theta-subgraph in H+eCH+e_{C} with the orientation DD, as shown in Figure 1.

More specifically, in Figure 1, the edge eC=u0​v0e_{C}=u_{0}v_{0}; the cycle CC, which is the union of the red directed path P1=(ui,ui−1,⋯,u0,v0,⋯,vk−1,vk)P_{1}=(u_{i},u_{i-1},\cdots,u_{0},v_{0},\cdots,v_{k-1},v_{k}) and the green directed path P2=(vk,vk+1,⋯,vl,ui)P_{2}=(v_{k},v_{k+1},\cdots,v_{l},u_{i}), and the cycle C1C_{1}, which is the union of the red directed path P1P_{1} and the blue directed path P3=(ui,ui+1,⋯,uj,vk)P_{3}=(u_{i},u_{i+1},\cdots,u_{j},v_{k}), are in H+eCH+e_{C} but not in HH; the cycle C2C_{2} is the common cycle of H+eCH+e_{C} and HH, formed by the union of both directed paths P2P_{2} and P3P_{3}. Then, to complete our proof, it suffices to show α⁡(C)=α⁡(C1)=α⁡(C2)=0\alpha(C)=\alpha(C_{1})=\alpha(C_{2})=0.

Since α\alpha is DD-admissible, we may assume α=αD,f\alpha=\alpha_{D,f} for some Abelian group Γ\Gamma and function f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma. Combining that CC and HH are α\alpha-compatible subgraphs of GG, this means

αD,f​(C)=α⁡(C)=0 and αD,f​(C2)=α⁡(C2)=0.\alpha_{D,f}(C)=\alpha(C)=0\quad\mbox{\rm~and~}\quad\alpha_{D,f}(C_{2})=\alpha(C_{2})=0.

This is further equivalent to satisfying the following equations

∑e∈E⁡(C)σD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=∑e∈E⁡(P1)σD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)+∑e∈E⁡(P2)σD⁡(C)​(e)​f​(e)=0\sum_{e\in E(C)}\sigma_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=\sum_{e\in E(P_{1})}\sigma_{D(C)}(e)f(e)+\sum_{e\in E(P_{2})}\sigma_{D(C)}(e)f(e)=0

and

∑e∈E⁡(C2)σD⁡(C2)​(e)​f​(e)=∑e∈E⁡(P2)σD⁡(C2)​(e)​f​(e)+∑e∈E⁡(P3)σD⁡(C2)​(e)​f​(e)=0.\sum_{e\in E(C_{2})}\sigma_{D(C_{2})}(e)f(e)=\sum_{e\in E(P_{2})}\sigma_{D(C_{2})}(e)f(e)+\sum_{e\in E(P_{3})}\sigma_{D(C_{2})}(e)f(e)=0.

Together with σD⁡(C1)​(e)=−σD⁡(C)​(e)\sigma_{D(C_{1})}(e)=-\sigma_{D(C)}(e) for any edge e∈E⁡(P1)e\in E(P_{1}) and σD⁡(C1)​(e)=σD⁡(C2)​(e)\sigma_{D(C_{1})}(e)=\sigma_{D(C_{2})}(e) for any edge e∈E⁡(P3)e\in E(P_{3}), we deduce

∑e∈E⁡(C1)σD⁡(C1)​(e)​f​(e)=∑e∈E⁡(P1)σD⁡(C1)​(e)​f​(e)+∑e∈E⁡(P3)σD⁡(C1)​(e)​f​(e)=0.\sum_{e\in E(C_{1})}\sigma_{D(C_{1})}(e)f(e)=\sum_{e\in E(P_{1})}\sigma_{D(C_{1})}(e)f(e)+\sum_{e\in E(P_{3})}\sigma_{D(C_{1})}(e)f(e)=0.

This implies α⁡(C1)=αD,f​(C1)=0\alpha(C_{1})=\alpha_{D,f}(C_{1})=0. Therefore, we conclude that H+eCH+e_{C} is an α\alpha-compatible subgraph of GG, which finishes the proof. ∎

We now return to the proof of the Generalized Whitney’s Broken Circuit Theorem when α\alpha is an admissible assigning.

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Suppose GG has q≥0q\geq 0 α\alpha-compatible broken cycles. For every α\alpha-compatible broken cycle BB, let eBe_{B} be the maximal member in BB with respect to the total order ≺\prec. We can arrange the α\alpha-compatible broken cycles B1,…,BqB_{1},\ldots,B_{q} such that eB1⪯eB2⋯⪯eBqe_{B_{1}}\preceq e_{B_{2}}\cdots\preceq e_{B_{q}}. Let 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} be the collection of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing the α\alpha-compatible broken cycle B1B_{1}. For i=2,…,qi=2,\ldots,q, let 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} be the collection of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing the α\alpha-compatible broken cycle BiB_{i} but not any of B1,…,Bi−1B_{1},\ldots,B_{i-1}. In addition, let 𝒮q+1\mathcal{S}_{q+1} be the collection of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG containing no α\alpha-compatible broken cycles. Then {𝒮1,𝒮2,…,𝒮q+1}\{\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{S}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{q+1}\} decomposes the set of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG. Combining Theorem 2.2, the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) can be written in the form

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑i=1q+1∑H∈𝒮i(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H).P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{i=1}^{q+1}\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}. (3.2)

We first consider 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. Assume B1=C1−eC1B_{1}=C_{1}-e_{C_{1}} for some α\alpha-compatible cycle C1C_{1} of GG, where eC1e_{C_{1}} is the maximal member in C1C_{1} with respect to ≺\prec. Clearly each member HH in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} containing eC1e_{C_{1}} gives rise to a unique member H−eC1H-e_{C_{1}} in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} that does not contain eC1e_{C_{1}}. Conversely, according to Lemma 3.3, each member HH in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} containing no eC1e_{C_{1}} gives rise to a unique member H+eC1H+e_{C_{1}} in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} containing eC1e_{C_{1}}. In addition, since B1+eC1=C1B_{1}+e_{C_{1}}=C_{1} is a cycle of GG, for each H∈𝒮1H\in\mathcal{S}_{1} containing eC1e_{C_{1}}, we have c⁡(H)=c⁡(H−eC1)c(H)=c(H-e_{C_{1}}). Thus, we derive

∑H∈𝒮1,eC1∈E⁡(H)((−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)+(−1)|E⁡(H)|−1​kc⁡(H−eC1))=0.\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{1},\,e_{C_{1}}\in E(H)}\big((-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}+(-1)^{|E(H)|-1}k^{c(H-e_{C_{1}})}\big)=0.

Namely, we arrive at ∑H∈𝒮1(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{1}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}=0 in (3.2).

Consider 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}. Assume B2=C2−eC2B_{2}=C_{2}-e_{C_{2}} for some α\alpha-compatible cycle C2C_{2} of GG, where eC2e_{C_{2}} is the maximal member in C2C_{2} with respect to ≺\prec. It follows from the ordering eB1⪯eB2e_{B_{1}}\preceq e_{B_{2}} that eB1⪯eB2≺eC2e_{B_{1}}\preceq e_{B_{2}}\prec e_{C_{2}}. So, B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} do not contain eC2e_{C_{2}}. Combining this, using the same argument as the case 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}, we conclude that every element HH in 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} containing no eC2e_{C_{2}} gives rise to a unique member H+eC2H+e_{C_{2}} in 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} containing eC2e_{C_{2}}, and vice versa. Hence, we also obtain ∑H∈𝒮2(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H)=0\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{2}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}=0 in (3.2).

Likewise, we can deduce the total contribution of the members in 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} to P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) is zero for each i=1,2,…,qi=1,2,\ldots,q. Therefore, P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) in (3.2) can be written as

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑H∈𝒮q+1(−1)|E⁡(H)|​kc⁡(H).P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{q+1}}(-1)^{|E(H)|}k^{c(H)}. (3.3)

Since every element H∈𝒮q+1H\in\mathcal{S}_{q+1} is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG and contains no α\alpha-compatible broken cycles, we can deduce that HH contains no cycles. Therefore, HH is a forest. This implies that for any member H∈𝒮q+1H\in\mathcal{S}_{q+1},

|E⁡(H)|≤r⁡(G) and c⁡(H)=|V⁡(G)|−|E⁡(H)|.|E(H)|\leq r(G)\quad\mbox{\rm~and~}\quad c(H)=|V(G)|-|E(H)|.

Thus, P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) in (3.3) can be further simplified to the following form

P⁡(G,α,k)=∑i=0r⁡(G)(−1)i​wi​(G,α)​k|V⁡(G)|−i,P(G,\alpha;k)=\sum_{i=0}^{r(G)}(-1)^{i}w_{i}(G,\alpha)k^{|V(G)|-i},

which finishes the proof. ∎

Furthermore, as a direct result of Theorem 3.2, we have the next corollary.

Corollary 3.4.

Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG. Then (−1)|V⁡(G)|​P​(G,α,−1)(-1)^{|V(G)|}P(G,\alpha;-1) is the number of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that do not contain α\alpha-compatible broken cycles.

Notably, every (Γ,0)(\Gamma,0)-coloring of GG is exactly a proper coloring of GG, vice versa. Therefore, when f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma is the zero function, P⁡(G,0,k)P(G,0;k) is precisely the classical chromatic polynomal P⁡(G,k)P\big(G;k\big) of GG. In this case, the 00-compatible spanning subgraph, 00-compatible cycle and 00-compatible broken cycle of GG correspond to the ordinary spanning subgraph, cycle and broken cycle of GG, respectively. Hence, Theorem 3.2 deduces the following Whitney’s Broken Cycle Theorem in [26] directly.

Theorem 3.5 ([26]).

Let ≺\prec be a total order on E⁡(G)E(G). Write the chromatic polynomial P⁡(G,k)P(G;k) as P⁡(G,k)=∑i=0r⁡(G)(−1)i​wi​(G)​k|V⁡(G)|−iP(G;k)=\sum_{i=0}^{r(G)}(-1)^{i}w_{i}(G)k^{|V(G)|-i}. Then each unsigned coefficient wi​(G)w_{i}(G) is the number of spanning subgraphs of GG that have exactly ii edges and do not contain broken cycles with respect to the total order ≺\prec.

4 Coefficient comparisons and further explorations

In this section, we primarily apply the Generalized Broken Cycle Theorem to explore how the coefficients of cycle-assigning polynomials vary with changes in assignings and to handle certain group coloring problems in graphs. We first establish a unified order-preserving relation from assignings to cycle-assigning polynomials when both are naturally ordered. Let α\alpha be an assigning of GG and ≺\prec be a total order on E⁡(G)E(G). For convenience, we denote by 𝒞⁡(G,α)\mathcal{C}(G,\alpha) and 𝒞′​(G,α)\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(G,\alpha) the sets of α\alpha-compatible cycles and α\alpha-compatible broken cycles of GG with respect to ≺\prec, respectively. Additionally, let 𝒞′′​(G,α)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha) represent the set of α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraphs of GG that do not contain α\alpha-compatible broken cycles with respect to ≺\prec.

Theorem 4.1 (Comparison of Coefficients).

Let α,α′\alpha,\alpha^{\prime} be two assignings of GG. If α⁡(C)≤α′​(C)\alpha(C)\leq\alpha^{\prime}(C) for all cycles C∈𝒞⁡(G)C\in\mathcal{C}(G), then the unsigned coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomials P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) and P⁡(G,α′,k)P(G,\alpha^{\prime};k) satisfy

wi​(G,α)≤wi​(G,α′) for i=0,1,…,r⁡(G).w_{i}(G,\alpha)\leq w_{i}(G,\alpha^{\prime})\quad\mbox{ for }\quad i=0,1,\ldots,r(G).

In particular, wi​(G)=wi​(G,0)≤wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G)=w_{i}(G,0)\leq w_{i}(G,\alpha) for any assigning α\alpha of GG.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.2, the proof reduces to showing that every member HH of 𝒞′′​(G,α)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha) belongs to 𝒞′′​(G,α′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). Given an element H∈𝒞′′​(G,α)H\in\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha). As HH is an α\alpha-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing no α\alpha-compatible broken cycles, this implies that HH does not contain cycles. Furthermore, since α⁡(C)≤α′​(C)\alpha(C)\leq\alpha^{\prime}(C) for any cycle of GG, we have 𝒞⁡(G,α)⊇𝒞⁡(G,α′)\mathcal{C}(G,\alpha)\supseteq\mathcal{C}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). This means 𝒞′​(G,α)⊇𝒞′​(G,α′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(G,\alpha)\supseteq\mathcal{C}^{\prime}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). This further deduces that HH does not contain α′\alpha^{\prime}-compatible broken cycles. Therefore, we conclude that HH is an α′\alpha^{\prime}-compatible spanning subgraph of GG containing no α′\alpha^{\prime}-compatible broken cycles. Namely, 𝒞′′​(G,α)⊆𝒞′′​(G,α′)\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha)\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime}(G,\alpha^{\prime}). ∎

When GG is a loopless graph, each unsigned coefficient wi​(G)w_{i}(G) of P⁡(G,k)P(G;k) is a positive integer, which is easily obtained from Theorem 3.5. Applying Theorem 4.1 to this, we can derive that for any loopless graphs GG, the coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) are nonzero and alternate in sign.

Corollary 4.2.

Let α\alpha be an assigining of GG. If GG is a loopless graph, then each unsigned coefficient wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) is a positive integer. Moreover, w0​(G,α)=1w_{0}(G,\alpha)=1.

It is well-known that the unimodality of the sequence wi​(G)w_{i}(G) was conjectured by Read [23], and the log-concavity was conjectured by Hoggar [9]. Both of these conjectures have been confirmed by Huh et al. [1, 10, 11]. Inspired by their work, we conjecture that the unsigned coefficients of the cycle-assigning polynomial P⁡(G,α,k)P(G,\alpha;k) form a log-concave, and hence unimodal, sequence for all loopless graphs.

Conjecture 4.3.

Let GG be a loopless graph and α\alpha be an assigning of GG. Then the sequence w0​(G,α),w1​(G,α),…,wr⁡(G)​(G,α)w_{0}(G,\alpha),w_{1}(G,\alpha),\ldots,w_{r(G)}(G,\alpha) satisfies the following properties:

  • •

    The sequence wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) is unimodal, i.e., there is an index 1≤j≤r⁡(G)1\leq j\leq r(G) such that

    w0​(G,α)≤⋯≤wj−1​(G,α)≤wj​(G,α)≥wj+1​(G,α)≥⋯≥wr⁡(G)​(G,α).w_{0}(G,\alpha)\leq\cdots\leq w_{j-1}(G,\alpha)\leq w_{j}(G,\alpha)\geq w_{j+1}(G,\alpha)\geq\cdots\geq w_{r(G)}(G,\alpha).
  • •

    The sequence wi​(G,α)w_{i}(G,\alpha) is log-concave, i.e, for j=1,…,r⁡(G)−1j=1,\ldots,r(G)-1,

    wj−1​(G,α)​wj+1​(G,α)≤wj​(G,α)2.w_{j-1}(G,\alpha)w_{j+1}(G,\alpha)\leq w_{j}(G,\alpha)^{2}.

It is a pleasant surprise that the Generalized Broken Cycle Theorem provides a new perspective on addressing certain group coloring problems in graphs. A well-known property in [25] says that if a graph has a nowhere-zero Γ\Gamma-flow, then it admits a nowhere-zero Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}-flow for any Abelian group Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} whose order is at least the order of Γ\Gamma. This does not extend to the more general concept of group connectivity observed by Jaeger et al. [12]. For a connected planar graph GG, Jaeger et al. [12] also showed that GG is Γ\Gamma-colorable if and only if the dual graph G∗G^{*} is Γ\Gamma-connected. Naturally, there is a corresponding problem in group colorings: for any Abelian groups Γ1\Gamma_{1} and Γ2\Gamma_{2} with the same order, is a Γ1\Gamma_{1}-colorable graph also Γ2\Gamma_{2}-colorable?

Most recently, Langhede and Thomassen in [19] confirmed that the property holds if Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} is sufficiently large compared to Γ\Gamma. This further implied that GG is always Γ\Gamma-colorable whenever Γ\Gamma has a sufficiently large order, which can be explained by the Generalized Broken Cycle Theorem. More specifically, note the basic fact that for a loopless graph GG, GG is Γ\Gamma-colorable for some Abelian group Γ\Gamma if and only if P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)>0P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)>0 for any f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma. This is also equivalent to saying that GG is Γ\Gamma-colorable if and only if P⁡(G,αG,f,|Γ|)>0P(G,\alpha_{G,f};|\Gamma|)>0 for any DD-admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} related to f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma. When GG is a loopless graph, it follows from Theorem 3.2 that w0​(G,α)=1w_{0}(G,\alpha)=1 for any assigning α\alpha of GG. Thus, P⁡(G,α,|Γ|)>0P(G,\alpha;|\Gamma|)>0 always hold for all assigning α\alpha of GG in this case whenever the Abelian group Γ\Gamma has a sufficiently large order.

We conclude this section with the following corollary, which is a direct consequence of the mentioned fact.

Corollary 4.4.

Let Γ,Γ′\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime} be two Abelian groups of the same order and GG a Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}-colorable graph. If each DD-admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} of GG with f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma is also a D′D^{\prime}-admissible assigning αD′,f′\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}} of GG for some f′:E⁡(G)→Γ′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to\Gamma^{\prime}, then GG is Γ\Gamma-colorable.

Proof.

Since GG is Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}-colorable, we have P⁡(D′​(G),f′,Γ′)>0P\big(D^{\prime}(G),f^{\prime};\Gamma^{\prime}\big)>0 for any f′:E⁡(G)→Γ′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to\Gamma^{\prime}. As each DD-admissible assigning αD,f\alpha_{D,f} with f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma is a D′D^{\prime}-admissible assigning αD′,f′\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}} of GG for some f′:E⁡(G)→Γ′f^{\prime}:E(G)\to\Gamma^{\prime}, it follows that for any f:E⁡(G)→Γf:E(G)\to\Gamma,

P⁡(D⁡(G),f,Γ)=P⁡(G,α,|Γ|)=P⁡(D′​(G),f′,Γ′)>0P\big(D(G),f;\Gamma\big)=P(G,\alpha;|\Gamma|)=P\big(D^{\prime}(G),f^{\prime};\Gamma^{\prime}\big)>0

via Corollary 2.3, where α=αD,f=αD′,f′\alpha=\alpha_{D,f}=\alpha_{D^{\prime},f^{\prime}}. This implies that GG is Γ\Gamma-colorable. ∎
